we identified and characterized a novel arginine finger in the pyrophosphorylase dUTPase that fulfills all of the criteria established for the arginine fingers in the nucleotide triphosphate hydrolases.
we identified and structurally characterized the arginine finger of pyrophosphatases, which is a highly conservatively positioned residue that is crucial for the catalytic mechanism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the structural features and functional properties of arginine fingers in pyrophosphatases and their comparison to the arginine fingers from GTPases and AAA+ ATPases.
the identification of an arginine finger for a pyrophosphatases and the characterization of its role in catalysis.

the characterization of an arginine finger that is used to cleave the γ-phosphate in the pyrophosphohydrolase dUTPase, and its comparison with analogous arginine fingers in nucleotide hydralases and transferases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

arginine fingers are not only used to stabilize the transition state of the reaction, but also to complete the active site by coordinating the nucleotide substrate and positioning its γ-phosphate for catalysis.

arginine fingers in pyrophosphatases are used to stabilize the γ-phosphate in the transition state, while the electrostatic interaction with the leaving pyrophosphate is the primary role of the arginine finger in NTPases.
the arginine finger is a versatile and essential residue that is used by many nucleotide hydrotases to stabilize the transition state and to complete the active site.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the arginine finger in dUTPases is a unique case of a nucleotide binding protein where the arginine finger is not directly involved in the transition state stabilization.
the arginine finger in pyrophosphatases has an essential role in the structural organization of the catalytic site, while its direct catalytic role is secondary.
we identified a novel type of arginine finger for the pyrophosphorylases, and we established the structural basis of the catalytic function of arginine fingers.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the arginine finger of dUTPase, as in other enzymes, has a structural role in the formation of the active site, but it also plays a direct catalytic role in stabilizing the transition state of pyrophosphate release.

a conserved, structurally equivalent, but chemically distinct arginine finger can be found in the active sites of many different enzymes, which is an example of how the same amino acid can perform different functions depending on the enzyme.
arginine finger is an essential structural component of the active site that is conserved across a wide range of hydrolase and transferase enzymes.
